metadata.title: Students' problem-solving skills in-depth: ready for ‘real life’?
metadata.venue: The International Journal of Management Education

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This study does not use an ILSA micro-dataset with sampling weights; instead, it analyzes 188 university group written assignments (paragraph-level coding) collected over six years. Because the data are not drawn from a complex survey design (students are not sampled via stratified/clustered national sampling frames), there is no reported application of student/sampling weights or replicate-weight methods. The analysis relies on qualitative-to-quantitative content coding (OECD PISA problem-solving processes) and reliability checks (Cohen’s Kappa) rather than weighted estimation of population parameters. Consequently, no weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) is applicable to the reported results.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values (PVs) are not applicable because the dependent variables are coded proportions of problem-solving processes/tasks in written university assignments, not cognitive achievement scores generated via PV-based scaling (as in PISA/TIMSS). Missing-data handling is not reported because the study does not describe item-level missingness typical of large-scale assessments; instead, it reports coding coverage at the paragraph level and reliability statistics. Therefore, the usual PV/missing-data documentation requirements for ILSA achievement modeling do not apply to this content-analysis design.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: A total of 188 group assignments were analyzed. The assignments were collected over six years (Semester 1 or 2 each year, plus one summer class) and each assignment was coded at the paragraph level according to the OECD PISA problem-solving framework processes (EU, RF, PE, MR) and the 21 core tasks. References and glossaries were excluded from paragraph counts and analysis; figures/tables were counted as described (e.g., tables as images counted as figures). The study does not report country-level sampling or student-level inclusion/exclusion beyond the assignment-level corpus and paragraph-level coding rules.

data.outcome_summary: This paper is a descriptive content-analysis study applying the OECD PISA problem-solving framework to management education: 188 university group assignments were coded at the paragraph level into four processes (EU, RF, PE, MR) and 21 core tasks. The results show strong evidence of EU and RF processes (EU: 3495 paragraphs, 43.25%; RF: 3232, 40.00%) and weaker evidence of PE and MR (PE: 19.28%; MR: 7.30%). Within core tasks, the highest coded proportion was MR3 (discussing solution impact for the decision maker/company), while weaker performance appeared for MR2 (other variables that could have been considered) and MR4 (limitations/restrictions). The study reports reliability using weighted Cohen’s Kappa (substantial agreement for EU/RF/PE; fair for MR). No machine-learning prediction model, PV-based achievement outcome, or survey-weighted estimation is used; therefore, findings describe observed alignment with the framework rather than predictive accuracy or causal effects.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The study does not perform machine-learning prediction/classification and does not use ILSA-style PV-based achievement outcomes; it instead codes written assessments against the OECD PISA problem-solving framework. As a result, fields related to ML techniques, PV handling for cognitive scores, and country-level ILSA sampling are not populated. The sample is described at the assignment/paragraph level (188 group assignments) rather than as an ILSA student microdata sample with country breakdowns.
